or_acker_rock.blurb: Acker Rock is a remote formation in the Umpqua National Forest, reached from Tiller by a long run of forest roads. It is an adventure destination more than a cragging stop: the faces are mostly slabs where friction counts, bolts are spaced well apart, and a light rack helps on the sport and trad lines alike. Grades run from easy fifth class up to the low 5.10s, with the bulk at 5.9 and below, so comfortable climbers can find plenty. Expect long pitches, multi-pitch ground and committing rappels, plus a lookout cabin on the summit. Bring two ropes and a mindset for self-reliance.

or_river_spot.blurb: River Spot is a small cluster of boulders at Cline Falls, a short drive west of Redmond, tucked in a downhill pocket close to the Deschutes River. It is part of the east side of the Main Area Boulders. The basalt problems run from very easy to very hard, with a handful of high-quality lines worth the walk and most of the rest in the V0 to V7 range, topped by one V9. Reach it by dropping down from the clearing under the power lines and following the trail downstream; the whole approach from the pullout takes around ten minutes.

or_gorilla_cliff.blurb: Gorilla Cliff is a boulder band beside the Bivy campground at Smith Rock, sitting a little below and upstream of the Bivy Wall. Regarded as the most popular bouldering at Smith, it holds a long run of problems from easy warm-ups to the double-digit grades, with a good number of V2 to V8 lines in the middle. Reaching it means walking past the Bivy Boulders and descending a flight of switchback steps, after which the cliff is on your left. Bring pads and spotters; stone at Smith ranges from solid to flaky.

or_the_cave.blurb: The Cave is the centrepiece of the Zoo, a small side area at Smith Rock, and you cannot miss it: a wide open grotto with a flat platform at its foot. The climbing is all sport, on very steep rock with oversized holds, which makes it one of the few places at Smith for cave-style training below the hardest grades. Routes start around 5.10 and mostly sit in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, with a few at 5.13. Many lines are fitted with fixed cable draws, and the large holds can be hard on the skin, so tape up. Quality is consistently praised.

or_1st_wall.blurb: The 1st Wall is part of the Williamson River Cliffs, a columnar basalt band above the river canyon north of Klamath Falls, east of Highway 97. Most of the climbs are traditional leads, with a handful of bolted lines and fixed anchors that make top-roping easy. Grades start at easy fifth class, cluster in the 5.6 to 5.10 range and reach into the 5.12s. A short trail leads from the lower parking area to the base. Views from the top take in the Klamath Basin and the river, and the wall faces south.

or_rockgarden_wall.blurb: Rockgarden Wall is the left-hand and bigger of the two main walls at Carver Cliff, a roughly 80-foot crag near Carver. Sport routes and traditional lines share the face in nearly equal numbers. Grades begin at moderate fifth class, but the wall is best known for its 5.11 and 5.12 leads, which make up most of the routes here, so it suits climbers who already climb solidly. A few moderate trad routes at 5.8 and 5.9 give less experienced leaders something to try.

or_monument_base_area_the.blurb: The Monument Base Area is the foot of the big Monument spire at Smith Rock, reached by crossing the footbridge and following the river for under ten minutes. The wall catches morning sun. Mostly bolted sport routes, with a few traditional lines and a couple of multi-pitch outings, cover grades from easy fifth class to the 5.12 range, with a strong cluster at 5.10 and 5.11. Development is recent in places, so loose rock is a worry and a helmet is sensible.
